data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism offers justificatory reasons for the preference that do not track corroboration at all, but instead track falsifiability — a distinct Popperian virtue. The mechanism states we prefer the theory 'because it is the best available target for future criticism and the most informative if false.' Both criteria — being a target for criticism and being informative if false — are properties of a theory's logical content (its falsifiability), not of its test history. A newly proposed, maximally falsifiable theory that has never been tested is maximally informative if false and an ideal target for future criticism, yet it is not corroborated at all. Conversely, a well-corroborated but narrow theory may be less informative if false than a bold untested rival. Thus the justificatory reasons the target supplies would, in cases like this, select the less-corroborated theory, directly contradicting the preference the claim purports to defend. The defense therefore fails to establish a Popperian rationale for preferring *better-corroborated* theories; it only establishes a rationale for preferring more *falsifiable* ones, which is a different and weaker claim. The target conflates corroboration (a report of past test-survival) with falsifiability/informativeness (a feature of logical form), leaving the stated mechanism unable to justify the stated preference.
